messages.content: You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "Mining Robots" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-2 Mining Robots (0B (pathfinder units in 0A))
Accepted scope: Tether-powered excavation robots at the target NEA, with onboard batteries for mobility and safe mode, plus replacements.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):

- T08 Particle containment, escape verification and tailings management: TRL 2–3 now, target 6, AD² 6–7, project-ending

- T21 Robotic maintenance, repair and spares logistics (GPT: and site installation and recovery): TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 6, project-ending
- T24 Dust-tolerant long-life mechanisms and seals: TRL 2–5 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, project-ending

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-2 Mining Robots: Technical Proposal

**Item:** bom-0-2 Mining Robots. Pathfinder units in 0A; production fleet in gated 0B.
**Baseline context:** Fe-Ni product co-located at the target NEA; SEL1 reference receiving node (D-04, interim); robots tether-powered from site power.
**Status:** Proposal for configuration control. All numbers are ranges with a stated basis. Confidence is stated per number. Nothing here is adopted until the owner accepts it.

---

## 0. Executive summary

I recommend a robot concept called the **Anchored Cell Excavator (ACE)**. Its main features:

- **Body and mobility.** It is a low, wide, wheel-less sled. It moves as a cable-driven parallel robot inside a pre-anchored work cell of about 30 m, using four on-board winches on four anchor lines.
- **Power.** It is fed by a ±1 kV DC bipolar tether (2 kV pole-to-pole) from a cell power node supplied under bom-0-5.
- **Excavation.** It collects fines with an enclosed pair of slow, counter-rotating, up-cut drums. The drums are arranged so their steady reaction pulls the head into the material rather than pushing the robot off the body.
- **Cobbles.** A second manipulator with a grab clears cobbles and services anchors and other robots.

The design follows five principles.

1. **On a rubble pile you cannot push on the ground.** The robot weighs about 0.1–0.5 N on a Bennu- or Itokawa-class body. At milli-g, digging is a load-path problem, not a power problem.
   - Every steady force must close inside the robot–material system.
   - Anchors must carry only pretension and bounded transients.
   - Slip clutches must cap transients below the anchor capacity actually demonstrated.
2. **Collect, don't mine.** The robot takes the <25 mm fines fraction at about 1:1 (per A4) and does no comminution. Competent ordinary-chondrite clasts are pushed aside, not cut.
   - This puts baseline electrical demand at about 2.5 kW average and 8 kW peak, not tens of kW.
3. **Size for the actual product.** Round 2 sized the fleet for a water-first chain. The binding baseline is native and reduced Fe-Ni, so the excavated tonnage is set by **metal grade × recovery**.
   - At 1.3 kt/yr product, 10 wt% metal and 60% recovery, the robots must deliver about **22 kt/yr** of run-of-mine fines.
4. **Nothing the robot does may exceed 0.25–0.3 v_esc.** This applies to the robot body and to anything the robot touches.
   - A robot that loses every anchor at maximum speed therefore stays gravitationally bound and recoverable.
   - Material the robot handles cannot be launched to escape by the robot's own kinematics.
5. **Buy evidence before replicas.**
   - 0A: two flight pathfinders, plus one ground qualification model under bom-0-11.
   - 0B: a fleet sized at KDP-0B from signed Phase 1 demand and measured pathfinder productivity. Reference: 8 delivered (6 active + 2 spare/servicing) and 3 later replacements.

**Cost (bom-0-2 recurring hardware only; low confidence):**

| | Range | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| 0A | $120–245M | $170M |
| 0B (gated) | $345–730M | $500M |

Robot-specific NRE is $300–650M (ref $450M) and is carried in **bom-0-11**, not here.

**Where I depart from the round-2 panel:**

- Fleet basis: Fe-Ni rather than water.
- Power: reject 25–70 kW as baseline.
- Mobility: reject walking and bucket wheels.
- Pathfinders: 2 rather than 3.
- Duty cycle: higher in 0B, lower in 0A.
- Velocity rule: tighter and body-relative.
- Test rig: no 10 kN·m stall rig.

Details are in §11.

---

## 1. What changes when the binding context is applied

| Driver | Round-2 assumption | Binding context | Consequence for robots |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Water-first (Claude W, GPT, Gemini) | Native/reduced Fe-Ni; water only as a C-type pilot (bom-0-6) | Tonnage is set by metal grade × recovery, not water wt% |
| Plant location | Disputed | Co-located at the target NEA | Short haul (≤50 m) to a sealed dock; no on-robot beneficiation |
| Power | Arrays vs tether disputed | HV tether, 1–3 kV, 10–50 kWh battery | Arrays on the robot are deleted. The robot is sized round tether and anchors |
| Delivered product | — | 0.6–2.5 kt/yr | Fleet range 3–16 robots across the full envelope (§3) |
| Crew | — | Uncrewed | Peer robotic servicing is a design driver (T21) |

---

## 2. Physical environment the design is built round

| Parameter | Design range | Basis / note |
|---|---|---|
| Body diameter | 0.3–1.5 km rubble pile | Typical accessible S-type NEA. Fe-Ni favours H/L-chondrite-like S-types |
| Surface gravity | 2×10⁻⁵ to 3×10⁻⁴ m/s² | Itokawa about 1×10⁻⁴; Bennu about 6×10⁻⁵ |
| Escape velocity | 0.15–0.6 m/s | Itokawa about 0.17 m/s; Bennu about 0.2 m/s; a 1 km S-type about 0.5 m/s |
| Robot weight on surface (2.65 t) | 0.05–0.8 N | Weight is negligible. Every load path is anchor- or inertia-limited |
| Surface-layer cohesion | 0–10 Pa design; up to 1 kPa at depth (unknown) | Gravity-regime cratering on Ryugu and very low resistance at Bennu TAG imply a near-cohesionless top layer. I side with Gemini's 0.1–10 Pa for the top 0.3 m, and design for Claude's ≤1 kPa only as an upper bound at depth |
| Fines (<25 mm) fraction in selected ponds | ≥60% by mass required | **Target-selection requirement, not an assumption.** Pushed to bom-0-1 and the target gate |
| Free metal in fines | 8–18 wt% acceptable; 10 wt% reference | H-chondrite-like. LL-like (about 2 wt%) targets do not close (§3) |
| Surface temperature | 200–400 K diurnal | About 1 AU; equator and mid-latitudes |
| Rotation period | 4–12 h | Night lasts 2–6 h. The tether lets robots work through night on site storage |
| Mid-latitude effective gravity | Must be >0 at site | Rules out near-critical equators on fast rotators. Site-selection requirement |

**The governing number.** A 50 N crowd force applied for 30 s to a free 2.65 t robot gives Δv ≈ 0.57 m/s, which exceeds escape velocity on every candidate. No design that relies on robot mass or ground bearing can work. Hence principle 1.

---

## 3. Fleet sizing for the Fe-Ni product

### 3.1 Excavation demand

M_exc = P / (g_m × η_r)

- P = delivered Fe-Ni product
- g_m = free-metal grade in the robot-delivered fines
- η_r = plant recovery to product specification (bom-0-3 owns this; I use it only for sizing)

| Case | P (kt/yr) | g_m | η_r | Yield | M_exc (kt/yr) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low demand, rich target | 0.6 | 18% | 80% | 14.4% | 4.2 |
| **Reference** | **1.3** | **10%** | **60%** | **6.0%** | **22** |
| High demand, reference target | 2.5 | 10% | 60% | 6.0% | 42 |
| Reference demand, lean target | 1.3 | 5% | 50% | 2.5% | 52 |
| LL-like target (reject) | 1.3 | 2% | 60% | 1.2% | 108 |

The reference tailings stream is about 21 kt/yr. This is consistent with GPT's 19.2 kt/yr (14–24 kt/yr).

### 3.2 Per-robot output

| Factor | 0A pathfinder (yr 1) | 0B reference | 0B range | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nameplate dig rate in fines | 1–2 t/h | 2.0 t/h | 1–3 t/h | §5.3: 2 drums × 0.6 m × 5 cm × 7 mm/s × 1.3 t/m³ ≈ 2 t/h |
| Fraction of an active hour spent digging | 0.4 | 0.6 | 0.5–0.7 | Hopper fill about 45 min, then about 25 min to dock and return |
| Availability (servicing, re-rigging, holds, faults) | 0.15–0.25 | 0.40 | 0.25–0.55 | Tethered, so not illumination-limited. Rigging is about 5% |
| Cutting hours per year | 400–1,000 | **2,000** | 1,000–3,000 | 8,760 × availability × dig fraction |
| Output per robot | 0.4–2 kt/yr | **4.0 kt/yr** | 1.0–7.5 kt/yr | — |

My 0B figure is above Claude's 1,500 h and Gemini's 1,300 h, for one reason. Under the binding tether-plus-site-storage architecture, robots are not illumination-limited. The 2–6 h nights on 4–12 h rotators are covered by site storage at about 20 kW fleet load: 40–120 kWh per night, against 0.5–15 MWh of site storage.

My 0A figure is deliberately low. First-flight robots spend most of their time on characterisation, not production.

### 3.3 Fleet

N_active = ⌈M_exc / O_robot⌉
N_delivered = N_active + ⌈0.33 × N_active⌉ (servicing rotation and peer-repair spares)

| Case | M_exc | N_active (at 4 kt/yr) | N_delivered | Replacements (5 yr) | Total 0B units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 4.2 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 4 |
| **Reference** | **22** | **6** | **8** | **3** | **11** |
| High | 42 | 11 | 14 | 4 | 18 (exceeds the 16 I would authorise; re-plan) |
| Lean target | 52 | 13 | 17 | 5 | Fails the economics gate; re-target |

**Replacements are derived from reliability, not forecast.** I side with GPT here.

- Reference loads: 6 active robots × 5 yr × about 4,000 operating h = 120,000 robot-hours.
- Target mission-ending failure rate after peer repair: 1 per 40,000 h. That gives about 3 losses.
- The range of 2–5 corresponds to an unrecoverable MTBF of 25,000–60,000 h.
- The bom-0-14 depot covers recoverable failures through LRU swaps.

**Recommendation.** Authorise 0B at the reference size of 8 + 3 only if the pathfinders demonstrate the KDP-0B productivity floor in §8.4. The final N is fixed at the gate under D-01.

---

## 4. Work-cell architecture

```
                      SITE PLAN (one active work cell, ~30 m across)

           A1 (boulder sling, >=2 m clast)              A2 (screw-umbrella pile)
             o------------------------------------------o
             |\                                        /|
             | \  anchor line L1         anchor line L2/ |
             |  \                                    /  |
             |   \        BENCH (unexcavated)       /   |
             |    \     +--------------------+     /    |
             |     \    |   ACE robot (sled) |    /     |       CPN = cell power node (bom-0-5)
             |      +===|  4 winches  [hopper]|===+      |       SD  = sealed dock (bom-0-3 inlet)
             |          +---------+----------+          |       ~~~ = HV/fibre tether (on robot reel)
             |                    | boom (4.5 m)        |
             |       .............v.............        |
             |       :  PAN (excavated, 0-1.5 m) :      |
             |       :   drum head works face   :       |
             |       :..........................:       |
             |      /                          \        |
             |     / L4                      L3 \       |
             o----/------------------------------\-----o
           A4  [SD]~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~[CPN]  A3
                 ^ sealed dock inside the anchor web, so the robot reaches it on its own lines

      Site guide-line network (fixed lines) links cells, the dock and the hub for inter-cell moves.
```

**How the cell works.**

- **Cell rigging.** Four perimeter anchors, A1–A4, sit 12–18 m from the cell centre.
  - Boulder slings (straps round embedded clasts ≥2 m) are the bootstrap type. They need manipulation only, no driving force.
  - Once two slings hold, the robot can react the torque of driving screw-umbrella piles against them.
- **Mobility.** The robot moves as a cable-driven parallel robot: four winches pay out and haul in four anchor lines. There are no wheels and no legs.
  - Speed limit is ≤0.25 v_esc of the body, i.e. 0.04–0.15 m/s.
  - Line pretension is 30–80 N.
- **Benching.** The robot sits on an unexcavated bench at anchor elevation and reaches down into the pan with its boom.
  - It never digs under itself. Otherwise the lines would angle upward and lift it.
  - One bench pass covers about 20 m × 6 m × 1.5 m ≈ 230 t, taking about 2–3 weeks.
  - One cell level holds about 1,400 t, i.e. about 3–4 months per robot.
  - The robot then re-rigs to the next level or cell.
- **Hopper cycle.** The robot travels on its own lines to the sealed dock inside the web and transfers through a double-door port, then returns. A dock sits ≤20 m from any working point.
- **Inter-cell moves** use fixed guide lines installed during site build. During site build the robots themselves rig the lines (T21 site installation).

**Why not walking or wheels.** Traction is proportional to weight, and weight is effectively zero.

- Walking hexapods with microspines need a grip capacity on rubble that nobody has demonstrated. They also add 12–18 actuated joints, each exposed to dust (T24).
- Cable-driven mobility puts all motion actuators inside the sealed body and makes every force on the robot a measured line tension.

---

## 5. The robot (ACE-1)

### 5.1 General arrangement

```

        radiator (edge-on to Sun, 2 x 3 m², EDS-coated)
                 ||
   lidar/stereo  ||                         manipulator (7-DOF, 3 m) + grab / tool changer
        [o]======||==========================\\
   +---------------------------------------------+      tether reel (350 m) + level-wind
   | avionics | battery 30 kWh | PMAD +/-1 kV   |~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ to CPN
   |----------+----------------+-------------- |
   | W1  W2 (winches)     HOPPER 1.2 m³  W3  W4 |----- anchor lines L1..L4
   |          [alpha-beta transfer port]       |
   +==================SKID (3.0 x 2.4 m)========+
   ////////////////// BENCH /////////////////// \
                                                \  boom (3-DOF, 4.5 m reach)
                                                 \
                                            +-----\------+
                                            | HOOD + brush|
                                            |  skirt      |
                                            | (D1)  (D2)  |  <- counter-rotating up-cut drums
                                            +-------------+     0.5 m dia x 0.6 m wide each
   ................... PAN FACE (fines) ..............
```

### 5.2 Principal specifications

| Dry mass, MEV (25% margin) | 2,650 kg | Allocation 1,800–3,500 kg | Low-medium | Margin per early-concept practice |

| On-board beneficiation | None (1:1) | 1.0–1.3 incidental from the grizzly | Medium | A4 |

### 5.3 Excavation head

| Item | Specification |
|---|---|
| Type | Enclosed counter-rotating drum pair (RASSOR lineage), **up-cut geometry** |
| Drums | 0.50 m diameter × 0.60 m wide each; 12 scoops each; 25 mm grizzly bars across scoop mouths |
| Speed | ≤2.0 rpm (ω ≈ 0.2 rad/s), giving tip speed ≤0.05 m/s on a 0.17 m/s body. The speed is scheduled to the measured v_esc of the target |
| Cut depth per pass | 3–8 cm (5 cm reference) |
| Advance speed | 4–10 mm/s (7 mm/s reference), set by boom and line pay-out |
| Steady drum torque (fines) | 3–30 N·m per drum (CBE). At 1–10 Pa cohesion, 10–100 N tangential at 0.25 m radius |
| Slip clutch | Adjustable 50–200 N·m per drum. **Set ≤50% of the demonstrated anchor transient capacity, referred to the head** |
| Motor and gear stall | 500 N·m per drum (over-rated for jam recovery, not for cutting) |
| Internal conveyance | Positive-displacement scoop-to-screw transfer into the hopper. **Gravity cannot be used**: the material is weightless |
| Mechanical power, fines | 20–200 W cutting and lifting; 200–600 W conveyance and seal friction |
| Electrical, head, typical | 0.5 kW (0.3–1.5) |
| Electrical, head, peak | 2 kW (jam reverse and clear) |
| Hood | Rigid enclosure. Brush and labyrinth skirt, 50 mm compliant stroke. Electrodynamic dust shield (EDS) on the window and sensor ports |
| Instrumentation | Six-axis F/T at the boom wrist; drum torque and speed; hood-internal particle imager; skirt-gap lidar |

**Why up-cut.** In the contact zone the scoops move upward and inward through the material. Material drag on the scoops therefore points down, so the head is *pulled into* the face.

- The boom holds the head back in tension.
- The reaction enters the robot as compression onto the skid and bench, not as uplift on the anchors.
- The two drums' horizontal components oppose each other.

**I do not credit any cancellation fraction (contra Gemini's 90–95%).** The residual six-axis load is a measured quantity. It is the T04 exit metric.

**What the head does not do.**

- It does not cut competent clasts. Ordinary-chondrite cobbles are tens to hundreds of MPa in strength, and cutting them would need multi-kW power and kN·m torques that no demonstrated anchor can react.
- The grizzly rejects anything over 25 mm. Cobbles of 25–400 mm (≤150 kg) are cleared by the grab into a windrow at the cell edge.
- Collection of cobbles for a plant crusher is a bom-0-3 decision. The grab and hopper can support it at about 0.5 t/h.

**Carried alternates (decided at the 0A downselect, §8):**

- **H-alt-1: sealed clamshell grab as primary collector.** Batch operation. Better containment and jam tolerance; lower rate, about 1–1.5 t/h.
- **H-alt-2: percussive comminution head** for boulder-dominated sites, at 5–10 kW. Only if the target gate forces it. The PMAD and tether already carry 15 kW for this reason.
- **Research only, not baselined (per A4): magnetic pick-up head.** Native Fe-Ni is ferromagnetic, so this is a potential beneficiation multiplier. It is tested on the pathfinder as an experiment.

### 5.4 Manipulator and grab

| Item | Specification |
|---|---|
| Arm | 7-DOF, 3.0 m reach, 300 N tip force continuous, 0.5–1.0 kN at the anchor tool |
| End effectors | Tool changer carrying a cobble grab (25–400 mm), sling installer, screw-pile driver (500 N·m, rotary with low-amplitude percussion), and servicing tools (LRU drivers, connector mates, cable handling) |
| Servicing interfaces | Standard robotic ORU interfaces on head, battery, reel, winch modules and avionics. Any ACE can swap any other ACE's LRUs (T21) |
| Power | 0.3 kW typical, 1.5 kW peak |

### 5.5 Anchoring and mobility (T16)

| Item | Specification | Note |
|---|---|---|
| On-board winches | 4 × capstan winch, 60 m line each, 0–0.15 m/s, tension-controlled to ±2 N | All drive elements inside the sealed body |
| Anchor lines | Vectran or aramid core with a braided stainless abrasion jacket. 5 kN break, 1 kN transient working, 200 N sustained working | Tension is logged at 1 kHz; slip is detected in <50 ms |

## 7. Containment (T08): robot-side allocation

bom-0-15 owns the site requirement and the ALARP ceiling (D-03). bom-0-2 proposes the following robot allocation, which uses velocity and enclosure as the verifiable controls.

| ID | Requirement | Value | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| MR-C1 | Tool-imparted particle velocity | ≤0.3 v_esc of the target, for all robot motions | Drop-tower and parabolic DEM validation; high-speed imaging in the pathfinder hood |
| MR-C2 | Body speed | ≤0.25 v_esc | Flight software limit, independently monitored |
| MR-C3 | Release outside the hood or hopper envelope, <1 mm grains, any velocity | ≤10 kg per robot per yr design goal (≈2.5 ppm of 4 kt/yr) | Witness plates, hood-skirt imager, mass balance (hopper vs dock) |
| MR-C4 | Release outside the envelope at >0.5 v_esc | ≤1 kg per robot per yr design goal | Inferred from MR-C1 and C3 distributions; witness-plate trajectory reconstruction |
| MR-C5 | Transfer-port release per dock cycle | ≤5 g | Vacuum-chamber cycle tests (≥2,000 cycles) |
| MR-C6 | Automatic stop rules | Stop the head when a hood-skirt gap exceeds 20 mm, a particle-imager count exceeds threshold, or a bom-0-15 site monitor alarms | Pathfinder |

**Reasoning.**

- I adopt Claude's position that mass fraction is the wrong governing variable.
- I tighten Claude's 0.5 v_esc to **0.3 v_esc for robot-imparted velocity**, because the plant and dock will add their own release mechanisms and need headroom.
- I reject Gemini's fixed 0.2 m/s. It roughly equals v_esc on Bennu-class bodies, so as a fixed number it protects nothing.
- MR-C3 and MR-C4 are allocations for bom-0-15, not standards. The ceiling itself goes to modelling and to the licensing state.

**Tailings.** Robots do not own tailings. The ACE hopper and port are, however, reversible: a robot can take a tailings load at the dock and place it in a mined-out pan as backfill. At the reference 21 kt/yr this needs about 5,000 robot-h/yr, equal to +2 robots ($56–120M). **I offer this to bom-0-15 as a priced option, not baselined scope.**

### 8.3 0A pathfinder fleet

**Two flight pathfinders (PF-1, PF-2), plus one QM on the ground (bom-0-11).** Not three flight units.

- 20 kW excavation: about one hour, but not an approved routine mode.

Longer shadow survival must be provided through site power, thermal design and an appropriate safe location—not by quietly expanding onboard storage.

Robot batteries count within the site storage total. Eight installed robots contain **0.24 MWh nominal**; the site energy balance must avoid counting that capacity twice.

### 7.3 Thermal rejection

Provide approximately **30 m² of deployed radiator area per robot**, with an initial trade range of **25–40 m²**.

This is based on rejecting approximately **10–15 kW** during sustained high-load operation at useful radiator temperatures around **330–350 K**, with conservative allowances for view factors, degradation and solar exclusion.

Important qualifications:
- Motor mechanical output partly leaves the robot through the material and substrate.
- Actual heat partition must be measured.
- Radiators require shielding from direct dust exposure and suitable solar orientation.
- Some duty points may require power derating.

No fixed excavated-material temperature rise is assumed.

### 7.4 Site power interface

For the reference installed fleet:
- Annual-average robot demand: **35–65 kW**.
- Allocated continuous branch capacity: **200 kW**.
- Short-duration coordinated peak: **250 kW**.

These values include housekeeping and charging but exclude the processing plant and shared site services. The site controller schedules high-power starts to prevent coincident transients.

---

## 8. Autonomy, control and communications

### 8.1 Control hierarchy

```text
Earth mission planning
        |
        v
Site production supervisor
        |
        v
Robot task executive
        |
        +--> restraint controller
        +--> excavation force/torque controller
        +--> enclosure and transfer controller
        +--> cable/mobility controller
        |
Independent safety controller
        |
Hardware shutdown, brakes, isolation, secure state
```

Earth approves work plans and operating envelopes. It does not close the excavation control loop.

### 8.2 Required autonomous capabilities

Each robot must:
- Execute bounded mining plans.
- Validate attachment before excavation.
- Regulate cutting loads.
- Detect inclusions and incipient jams.
- Withdraw or reverse tools safely.
- Maintain enclosure integrity.
- Exchange containers without material release.
- Recognize cable anomalies.
- Diagnose common faults.
- Request assistance from another robot.
- Remain mechanically secure during communications loss.

Suggested control rates:
- Motor and current loops: **1–10 kHz**.
- Force/torque control: **100–500 Hz**.
- Mobility and geometry updates: **10–50 Hz**.
- Supervisory planning: **0.1–1 Hz**.

### 8.3 Safety architecture

Use an independent safety controller with:
- Separate watchdog.
- Direct access to critical load and attachment sensors.
- Authority to disable drives and isolate HV.
- Validated safe-state sequences.
- Event recording independent of the main autonomy computer.

Machine-learning perception may support terrain and anomaly interpretation. It should not be the sole basis for load-limit enforcement or containment interlocks.

### 8.4 Communications

Initial allocations:
- Site-local robot links: **1–10 Mbps per active robot**, with burst capacity.
- Robot science/engineering data retained: **1–5 GB/day per active robot**.
- Mining-fleet Earth delivery: **5–30 GB/day**, selectively downlinked.
- Low-rate emergency telemetry on a separate robust path.

These are traffic requirements to bom-0-9, not a purchase of ground service within bom-0-2. Full-rate continuous video to Earth is unnecessary.

Qualify autonomous operation through at least a **seven-day planned communications outage**, with a longer safe-survival interval set by target geometry and energy analysis.

---

## 9. Maintenance and manufacturing

### 9.1 Maintenance strategy

Design for robotic exchange of:
- Excavation head.
- Tooth or cutter cassette.
- Drive module.
- Contact skirt and seal cassette.
- Transfer valve module.
- Sensor window.
- Tether termination.
- Power-conversion module.
- Battery module.

Use:
- Captive fasteners.
- Standardized grapple features.
- Coarse alignment guides.
- Contamination-isolated connectors.
- Visible configuration markings.
- Reversible assembly sequences.

Avoid field procedures requiring loose small parts, wire repair, fluid replenishment or precision manual alignment.

Two production robots should be able to assist each other. A failed robot must not become the sole obstruction to a feed route or power corridor.

### 9.2 Wear qualification

Do not specify a 20,000-hour cutting life without supporting evidence.

For the reference duty:
- Five-year productive cutting allocation: **5,500 hours**.
- Teeth, skirts, seals and some bearings are replaceable consumables.
- Qualification should establish replacement distributions and allowable inspection intervals.

Accelerated testing must preserve relevant wear mechanisms. Simply increasing abrasive concentration or speed can produce misleading life estimates.

### 9.3 Manufacturing approach

Use a common bus with target-specific end effectors and restraint kits.

Recommended production sequence:
1. Ground engineering units.
2. Two flight pathfinders.
3. Two production first articles.
4. Acceptance review using flight and endurance evidence.
5. Remaining initial production fleet.
6. Conditional replacement lots.

Common parts should include motors, controllers, sensors, valve actuators and exchange interfaces where technically justified.

Materials and processes require qualification for:
- Vacuum lubrication.
- Dust abrasion.
- Thermal cycling.
- Cold welding and galling.
- Electrical charging.
- Radiation.
- Long dormant storage before deployment.

Commercial industrial components may inform design, but terrestrial heritage does not establish relevant-environment readiness.

---

## 10. Scope boundaries and interfaces

| Interface | bom-0-2 responsibility | Other-item responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Prospecting | State excavation and attachment data requirements | bom-0-1 characterizes candidate targets |
| Processing | Deliver contained feed; provide composition and mass metadata | bom-0-3 owns processing from accepted inlet |
| Power | Onboard conversion, robot-carried tether and reel | bom-0-5 owns generation, storage and common distribution |
| Delivery | Robot packaging and deployment interfaces | bom-0-8 owns launch, cruise, landing and delivery |
| Communications | Robot terminals and data products | bom-0-9 owns site/network and Earth segment |
| Operations | Robot procedures, autonomy and diagnostics | bom-0-10 owns operational staffing and execution |
| Qualification | Technical requirements and test articles | bom-0-11 funds allocated NRE and qualification |
| Pathfinder | Robot design and supplied flight hardware | bom-0-12 owns integrated demonstration mission |
| Replacements | Whole replacement robots and robot-specific exchange kits costed here | bom-0-14 excludes those same articles; owns other common spares |
| Contamination | Robot enclosure and local sensing | bom-0-15 owns site-wide transport analysis, monitoring and containment integration |
| Authorization | Supply evidence and operational limits | bom-0-7 owns jurisdiction-specific authorization and assurance |

**Accounting rule:** Whole replacement robots are included in this proposal’s bom-0-2 total. If programme accounting places them under bom-0-14, transfer the cost rather than adding it again.

Site hubs, common cranes, permanent anchor infrastructure, container fleets and tailings installations require named owners and controlled interfaces. They are not implicitly included in a robot unit price.

---

## 11. Development roadmap and readiness gates

### 11.1 Technology status

Use the supplied panel TRL envelope; do not upgrade it based on this paper design.

| Technology | Current envelope | Principal qualification issue |
|---|---:|---|
| T04 excavation | TRL 2–3 | Rate, loads and energy on representative material |
| T08 containment/tailings | TRL 2–3 | Full-cycle release and credible escape verification |
| T09 HV tethers/distribution | TRL 2–4 | Dust, abrasion, charging, arcs and recovery |
| T10 autonomy | TRL 2–4 | Long-duration integrated fault handling |
| T16 anchoring/mobility | TRL 2–4 | Repeated loading in low-cohesion material |
| T21 maintenance/installation | TRL 2–4 | Autonomous exchange and recovery |
| T24 mechanisms/seals | TRL 2–5 | Relevant abrasive and thermal life |

### 11.2 Proposed sequence

Durations below are planning ranges and may overlap. Flight opportunities and target accessibility dominate calendar scheduling.

**Stage A — Requirements and discriminating experiments: 18–30 months**
- Compare excavation concepts.
- Establish six-axis load distributions.
- Test attachment concepts.
- Measure containment leakage.
- Establish material-property envelopes.
- Demonstrate integrated TRL 4 capabilities.

**Stage B — Integrated ground qualification development: 24–42 months**
- Full-scale thermal-vacuum excavation.
- Restrained microgravity analogues.
- Cable deployment and recovery.
- Robotic maintenance trials.
- Long-duration abrasive testing.
- TRL 5 demonstrations.

**Stage C — 0A flight pathfinders**
- Two robots with complementary instrumented tool configurations.
- Representative attachment, excavation, containment and transfer operations.
- At least one substantial maintenance or module-exchange demonstration.
- Operation through representative thermal and communications conditions.

**Stage D — KDP-0B**
No production commitment until the target, demand, economics and licence gates close.

### 11.3 KDP-0B evidence

For each project-ending technology, require **TRL 6 in a relevant environment, with no waivers**, as directed by D-02.

For this item, evidence must include:
- Excavation at representative depth and material properties.
- Demonstrated restraint margins under measured transients.
- Credible particle-release bounds.
- Sustained integrated autonomy.
- Relevant wear and seal-life evidence.
- Demonstrated robotic installation, recovery and maintenance.

Because T09 is an architecture-changing dependency, I would also require **TRL 6 for the selected HV tether implementation** before committing to the tether-dependent production fleet.

A pathfinder merely touching or briefly collecting surface material does not satisfy these requirements.

---

## 12. Cost analysis

### 12.1 Estimate basis

All costs are **constant 2026 US dollars**, order-of-magnitude engineering allowances:
- No supplier quotations.
- No assumed large-volume learning curve.
- No launch or delivery included in unit price.
- No common site infrastructure included.
- No programme contingency included.
- Production recurring prices assume successful completion of qualification.

### 12.2 0A costs

| Element | Quantity | Allowance | Accounting owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Flight pathfinder robot hardware, including unusual instrumentation | 2 | **$90–160M total** | bom-0-12 |
| Robot-attributable NRE, prototypes and qualification development | One development programme, predominantly 0A | **$400–850M** | bom-0-11 |
| Integrated flight mission, delivery, communications and operations | Mission dependent | Not estimated here | Respective shared items |

The $400–850M NRE allowance includes the robot-related excavation, restraint, autonomy, mechanism and local containment development. It does not purchase the entire site-wide debris-control programme.

**These values are attributable to mining capability, but must not be added again as direct bom-0-2 production procurement.**

### 12.3 0B recurring procurement

| Element | Quantity | Unit allowance | Extended allowance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Initial operating robots | 6 | $35–65M | $210–390M |
| Installed reserve robots | 2 | $35–65M | $70–130M |
| Conditional whole-robot replacements | 2–4 | $35–65M | $70–260M |
| Robot-specific exchange kits, acceptance fixtures and fleet accessories | One allowance | — | $20–45M |
| **Total recurring procurement** | **10–12 robots plus kits** | | **$370–825M** |

Initial eight-robot procurement, before replacements and accessories: **$280–520M**.

Whole replacement robots are an allowance, not a prediction that two to four robots will be lost. Replacement release should follow reliability evidence and mission duration.

### 12.4 Reconciliation with round-2 proposals

**Fleet quantity:**  
I recommend six working robots, two ready reserves, and two to four conditional replacements.

- This is close to the smaller round-2 fleets.
- I do not support 20 production robots before measured feed yield and productivity justify them.
- I also do not support assuming six replacements are necessarily required.

**Mass:**  
The proposed 3.4 t reference is above the lighter 2.5–2.8 t concepts because it explicitly allocates substantial restraint, enclosure, thermal-control and serviceability hardware.

**Power:**  
I do not endorse either a high-confidence 8 kW electrical requirement or 25–70 kW as the production baseline. The proposed **12–20 kW operating range** is a testable allocation, with **30 kW continuous service capability** and a higher development envelope.

**Cost:**  
The quoted $30–80M-class round-2 figures are plausible only as **recurring unit prices**, not as complete fleet or capability-programme costs. A $30–80M total programme cannot credibly procure, qualify and operate this fleet.

**Confidence:**  
Low for total cost and productivity; medium-low for the preliminary mass and power allocations.

---

## 13. Principal risks and responses

| Risk | Consequence | Response / decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| Accessible Fe–Ni yield below assumption | Excess feed and residue; fleet growth | Target gate based on representative samples and integrated recovery |
| Weak or unstable attachment substrate | Robot loss or inability to excavate | Multiple restraint concepts; verified work cells; reject unsuitable sites |
| Competent metallic inclusions | Jams, tool damage, low production | Instrumented load limiting; alternate head; no assumed hard-rock capability |
| Enclosure boundary leaks | Contamination or licence failure | Treat as project-ending until relevant-environment demonstration |
| Tether abrasion or charging | Power interruption, arcing | Managed routes, isolation, inspection and replaceable segments |
| Wear exceeds prediction | Replacement demand and outage growth | Endurance tests and replaceable wear cassettes |
| Autonomy common-mode failure | Fleet-wide outage | Independent safety logic; staged software deployment; replay testing |
| Service operations release dust | Production-compliant system fails lifecycle requirement | Include maintenance and faults in release verification |
| Insufficient heat rejection | Persistent derating | Early thermal-vacuum testing and explicit radiator reserve |
| Reserve robots share design defect | Reserves provide little protection | Reliability model must include common-cause failures |
| Demand does not materialize | Stranded production capital | Hold 0B; require signed material/purity/date demand |
| Relevant technology does not reach TRL 6 | Production cannot be authorized | Stop, redesign or defer; no readiness waiver |

A major programme risk is assuming that replication solves an unsuitable excavation architecture. **More robots do not compensate for failed restraint, unacceptable particle release or inaccessible metal.**

---

## 14. Open engineering questions

Before preliminary design review:

1. **What is the accessible feedstock?**  
   Loose grains, metal-bearing rubble and coherent metallic bodies require different machines.

2. **What attachment geometry is available?**  
   Strength alone is insufficient; shape, block mobility and cyclic stability matter.

3. **What is the relevant cutting-energy distribution?**  
   Measure both typical material and rare hard inclusions.

4. **Can the face enclosure maintain its release budget through repositioning and servicing?**

5. **What radiator geometry remains effective at the selected latitude, rotation period and solar distance?**

6. **What fraction of annual time is lost to container handling, cable management and attachment verification?**

7. **What maintenance tasks can another production robot actually perform?**

8. **How will kilogram-scale release bounds be verified despite much larger handled masses?**

Before KDP-0B:

9. What Phase 1 composition, inclusion, contamination, geometry and delivery-date specifications apply?

10. Does the selected target support conservative effective yield sufficient for the contracted demand?

11. What national authorization pathway and operating conditions apply?

12. Does the integrated mining-processing-delivery chain remain viable against Earth-supplied material?

13. Are replacement production lead times shorter than the demonstrated reserve coverage?

---

## 15. Recommendation

Fund the mining capability through **0A**, with two instrumented flight robots and a disciplined ground programme. Freeze the interface architecture now, but do not freeze the excavation head, anchor design or production fleet quantity before target evidence exists.

For 0B planning, carry:
- **Six operating robots.**
- **Two installed reserves.**
- **Two to four conditional replacements.**
- **3.4 t reference dry mass per robot.**
- **2 kV tether power and 30 kWh onboard battery.**
- **2 t/h reference productive rate.**
- **$370–825M recurring fleet allowance**, with development and shared infrastructure accounted elsewhere.

The decisive accomplishment is not a high instantaneous digging rate. It is a demonstrated, maintainable and licensable chain from **secure attachment to contained feed delivery**, at the duty cycle and effective metal yield needed by a real customer.

---

# bom-0-2 Mining Robots: Consensus Synthesis (Phase 0, revised architecture)

## Key Specifications

All three models agree on the following points.

- **Tether power at 2 kV DC.** Claude specifies ±1 kV bipolar (2 kV pole-to-pole); Gemini and GPT specify 2 kV nominal. All three keep this inside the binding 1–3 kV envelope. Site generation, storage and power nodes belong to bom-0-5; the robot carries its own tether, reel and DC-DC conversion. GPT and Claude add explicitly that the electrical tether is never a load-bearing or safety line.
- **30 kWh onboard battery.** Usable capacity is about 20–24 kWh (Claude 24, GPT 20–23, Gemini LTO chemistry). It covers mobility, tether-loss safe-hold and recovery. Claude and GPT state outright that routine production digging on battery is not baselined.
- **Excavation head.** The reference is an enclosed counter-rotating or opposed drum pair: Claude's up-cut drums, Gemini's dual bucket drums, GPT's opposed-drum candidate. Nameplate rate is about **2 t/h, with a range of 1–3 t/h**; Gemini gives 1.5–2.5. All three expect to downselect against alternates (grab, coring, scraping) during 0A.
- **Unbeneficiated feed through a sealed interface.** Fines go to bom-0-3 unbeneficiated (1:1). Transfer is through sealed containers or a double-door port, never open hopper transfer.
- **Robot mass of about 2.65–3.4 t dry.** Claude gives 2,650 kg MEV, Gemini 2,800 kg and GPT 3,400 kg. The excavation head is allocated 240–550 kg. The stowed envelope is about 3–3.5 m × 2.2–2.4 m.
- **Production fleet of about 6 robots plus reserves, not 20.**
  - Claude: 6 active + 2 spare + 3 replacements.
  - GPT: 6 operating + 2 reserve + 2–4 conditional replacements.
  - Gemini: 5 new 0B units plus 2 spares, alongside its 3 pathfinders. This implicitly withdraws its own round-2 figure of 20.
  - Final N is fixed at KDP-0B from signed Phase 1 demand and measured pathfinder productivity.
- **Recurring unit cost of about $28–65M per production robot.** Robot NRE is $300–850M and is carried outside the bom-0-2 recurring line, except that Gemini folds it into its 0A budget. Claude and GPT state, and Gemini's own figures imply, that the round-2 **$30–80M is only plausible as a unit price**, not as a fleet or programme cost.
- **Containment governed by more than mass fraction.** Particle velocity or kinematic limits plus enclosure are the controls, and site-wide ownership sits with bom-0-15 under the D-03 ALARP interim ceiling.
- **Precursor anchoring and geotechnical data before pathfinder build.** Claude recommends a 20–40 kg anchor-pull and penetrometer package on ≥2 bom-0-1 scouts. Gemini proposes a precursor penetrometer probe. GPT states attachment-data requirements that bom-0-1 must satisfy.

## Divergent Views

- **0A pathfinder count**
  - Claude recommends 2 flight units plus 1 ground QM (in bom-0-11). Its reason is that a peer-servicing pair is needed to retire T21, and a QM tested to failure is worth more than a third flight unit.
  - Gemini prefers 3 flight pathfinders at about $50M each ($150M).
  - GPT suggests 2 instrumented flight pathfinders at $90–160M total, preceded by ground prototypes.
- **Electrical power and heat rejection**
  - Claude recommends 2.5 kW average and 8 kW peak, with tether and PMAD rated to 15 kW for growth. Radiators are about 2 × 3 m² rejecting 1–1.5 kW.
  - Gemini prefers a 25 kW excavation peak and 3–5 kW for tramming.
  - GPT suggests 12–20 kW while excavating, a 30 kW continuous rating and a 40 kW peak (10 s). Radiators are about 30 m² rejecting 10–15 kW. GPT allocates 200 kW of site branch capacity for the fleet.
- **Mobility and anchoring**
  - Claude recommends a wheel-less sled moved as a cable-driven parallel robot inside pre-anchored 30 m cells. Anchors are boulder slings and screw-umbrella piles. The viability threshold is ≥200 N sustained and ≥1 kN transient per anchor.
  - Gemini prefers a hexapod with micro-spine feet rated >500 N holding force.
  - GPT suggests winch-assisted restrained repositioning with multiple attachment modes (bands, clamps, drilled anchors, reaction frames). Its restraint allocation is much larger: 10 kN working resultant, 15 kN·m moment and 5 kN transient.
- **Drum torque, tip speed and reaction cancellation**
  - Claude recommends ≤2 rpm and ≤0.05 m/s tip speed scheduled to v_esc. Steady torque is 3–30 N·m, with a 50–200 N·m clutch and 500 N·m stall. No cancellation fraction is credited.
  - Gemini credits 90–95% reaction-torque cancellation at a ≤0.2 m/s tip speed.
  - GPT suggests 0.2 m/s tip speed with 2–8 kN·m normal and 12 kN·m jam torque per drum, also with no cancellation credit.
- **Containment rule**
  - Claude recommends body-relative limits: ≤0.3 v_esc for tool-imparted particle velocity and ≤0.25 v_esc for body speed. Its release allocation is ≤10 kg per robot per year, of which ≤1 kg may be at >0.5 v_esc.
  - Gemini prefers a fixed mechanical tip-speed governor of ≤0.2 m/s.
  - GPT suggests a site ceiling of 100 kg/yr, with 60 kg/yr allocated to mining and a 10 kg/yr escape analysis target. It holds that tip speed is not a particle-release limit.
- **Duty and 0B cost**
  - Claude recommends 2,000 cutting h/yr in 0B (400–1,000 h in 0A), giving about 4 kt/yr per robot. Its 0B cost is $345–730M for 8 + 3 robots.
  - Gemini prefers about 1,800 h/yr and 3 kt/yr per robot. Its 0B cost is $250–300M.
  - GPT suggests 1,100 h/yr (12.6% of calendar time). Its 0B cost is $370–825M for 10–12 robots.

## Open Questions

1. **Real anchor capacity under cyclic load in target rubble.** This is the dominant project-ending unknown (T16). Claude rates the likelihood of failing 200 N sustained at 40–60%, and it sets clutch limits, cut depth and dig rate.
2. **Accessible free-metal grade and how it partitions by size.** Effective yield of about 2.5–15% moves excavation demand from about 4 kt/yr to over 50 kt/yr. If the metal sits in coarse clasts or coherent masses, a different head or a plant crusher is needed.
3. **Enclosure-to-natural-surface seal and release verification.** Can kilogram-scale release bounds be demonstrated, with upper confidence limits, against kiloton-scale flows? The verification must cover repositioning, servicing and faults, and electrostatic lofting must be characterised.
4. **Residual six-axis head loads.** Does counter-rotating or up-cut geometry actually produce net bearing rather than uplift in pascal-cohesion fines? Neither the 90–95% cancellation claim nor any other figure is yet supported by measurement.
5. **HV tether snag, abrasion and partial discharge on boulder fields.** Abrasion and partial discharge must be checked with dust and plasma charging present. The allowed snag rate and maximum tether length (50–350 m) are unresolved.
6. **Seal and port wear life in vacuum abrasive fines, and real peer-servicing capability.** Wear sets LRU intervals (500–3,000 h), the bom-0-14 spares demand and the true replacement count.

## Recommended Approach

1. **Fund 0A bom-0-2 at 2 instrumented flight pathfinders.** The cost is about $90–245M for hardware including research instrumentation. Add 1 ground QM for test-to-failure and concurrent life testing, funded in bom-0-11.
   - Reject Gemini's third flight unit. Two units are the minimum to demonstrate peer LRU swaps (T21) and still tolerate one loss.
   - Carry robot NRE of $300–850M in bom-0-11. Do not double-count it in bom-0-2.
2. **Hold 0B as a gated option sized by formula, not forecast.**
   - Size excavation demand as M_exc = P / (g·r·a·d), with N_active = ⌈M_exc / measured per-robot output⌉.
   - The planning reference is **6 active + 2 reserve, plus 2–4 reliability-derived replacements (10–12 total), costing about $280–825M recurring.**
   - Cap the fleet at about 16. Above that, re-target rather than scale.
   - This replaces all three round-2 figures. Gemini's 20 has no Fe-Ni closure. GPT's 6 replacements on 6 is an unsupported loss forecast. The round-2 $30–80M totals are unit prices.
3. **Freeze the interfaces now, but not the head, anchors or fleet size.**
   - Freeze the 2 kV DC tether and 30 kWh battery for safe mode and recovery only, with no production digging on battery.
   - Freeze sealed transfer with the robot specifying its hopper and port. bom-0-3 owns container and surge sizing in its 0.5–2 t trade range.
   - Downselect the head (enclosed drums, sealed grab, coring) and the mobility concept (cable-driven cell, restrained winch, legged) at PDR, using six-axis vacuum test data.
4. **Bound the power and thermal allocation to cover the model spread until measured.**
   - Rate the robot PMAD and tether at 15–30 kW.
   - Design radiators for the upper case with derating as the fallback.
   - Have bom-0-5 carry about 120–200 kW of fleet branch capacity until pathfinder data narrows it.
   - Credit no torque cancellation in any load case.
5. **Make anchoring the first-retired risk.**
   - Fly an anchor-pull and penetrometer package on ≥2 bom-0-1 scouts before pathfinder CDR.
   - Adopt Claude's thresholds as KDP-0B criteria: P10 ≥200 N sustained and ≥1 kN transient over ≥30 anchors, with a 100 N concept-break threshold triggering a grab head or target rejection.
6. **Adopt layered containment controls as the robot allocation to bom-0-15 under the D-03 interim ceiling.**
   - Use body-relative kinematic limits (≤0.25 v_esc body, ≤0.3 v_esc tool-imparted) in place of a fixed 0.2 m/s, which approximately equals v_esc on Bennu-class bodies.
   - Add per-robot kg/yr release allocations consistent with GPT's site budget (about 60 kg/yr for mining) and automatic stop rules.
   - Verify with upper-bound methods that include maintenance and fault releases.
7. **Set quantitative KDP-0B exit criteria with no waivers (D-02).** Each project-ending technology must reach TRL 6 at the target. T09 must also reach TRL 6, even though it is architecture-changing, because the fleet depends on tethers. The criteria are:
   - sustained dig rate ≥1.25 t/h over ≥200 cutting h;
   - extrapolated output ≥2.5 kt/yr per robot;
   - ≥95% intervention-free cutting hours;
   - ≥3 peer LRU swaps;
   - ≤1 snag-stop per 100 m of tether;
   - wear supporting ≥1,000 h LRU intervals;
   - bom-0-3 feed acceptance at an 8–18 wt% metal grade.
